rewritten_text:
“What’s wrong?” Oliver asked.

“Quiet!” the Dodger answered. “See that old fellow by the bookstall?”

“The old gentleman across the street?” said Oliver. “Yes, I see him.”

“He’ll do,” the Dodger said.

“A perfect target,” remarked young Charley Bates.

Oliver looked from one boy to the other in great surprise. But before he could ask anything, they crept across the road and slipped close behind the old gentleman they had pointed out. Oliver followed them for a few steps. Then, unsure whether to go on or turn back, he stopped and watched in silent amazement.

The old gentleman looked very respectable, with powdered hair and gold spectacles. He wore a dark green coat with a black velvet collar and white trousers, and carried a fine bamboo cane under his arm. He had picked up a book from the stall and stood reading it as intently as though he were sitting in his armchair in his own study. Perhaps he actually imagined himself there. He was plainly so absorbed that he noticed neither the stall, the street, nor the boys—nothing, in fact, except the book. He was reading it straight through, turning each page when he reached the bottom, starting at the first line of the next, and continuing steadily with the greatest interest and eagerness.

Imagine Oliver’s horror and alarm as he stood a few steps away, his eyes open as wide as they could go, and watched the Dodger thrust a hand into the old gentleman’s pocket and pull out a handkerchief! He saw him pass it to Charley Bates, and then saw both boys race around the corner as fast as they could run!

In a flash, the whole mystery of the handkerchiefs, the watches, the jewels, and the Jew became clear to Oliver.

For a moment he stood still, terror making the blood tingle so fiercely through his veins that he felt as though he were standing in a fire. Then, bewildered and frightened, he ran. Hardly knowing what he was doing, he fled as quickly as his feet would carry him.

All this happened within a minute. At the very moment Oliver started running, the old gentleman reached into his pocket, found his handkerchief gone, and spun around. Seeing the boy dashing away so fast, he quite naturally decided that Oliver was the thief. Shouting “Stop thief!” at the top of his voice, he hurried after him with the book still in his hand.

P.S.—Please tell me about the bows. Jennings insists they are fashionable.

Lord Arthur looked so serious and miserable as he read the letter that the Duchess burst out laughing.

“My dear Arthur,” she cried, “I shall never show you a young lady’s letter again! But what should I say about the clock? I think it is a wonderful invention, and I would like one myself.”

“I don’t think much of them,” Lord Arthur said with a sad smile. He kissed his mother and left the room.

Upstairs, he threw himself onto a sofa, his eyes filling with tears. He had tried his best to commit this murder, but both attempts had failed through no fault of his own. He had tried to do his duty, yet Destiny herself seemed to have betrayed him. He felt weighed down by the uselessness of good intentions and the pointlessness of trying to behave nobly. Perhaps he should call off the marriage altogether. Sybil would suffer, certainly, but suffering could not truly damage so noble a character. As for himself, what did it matter? There was always a war in which a man could die, a cause for which he could give his life. Since life offered him no pleasure, death held no terror. Let Destiny bring about his end. He would do nothing to help her.

At half past seven he dressed and went to the club. Surbiton was there with a group of young men, and he had to dine with them. Their shallow conversation and pointless jokes held no interest for him. As soon as coffee arrived, he invented an appointment and left. On his way out, the hall porter handed him a letter from Herr Winckelkopf. It asked him to visit the following evening to inspect an explosive umbrella that went off as soon as someone opened it. This was the latest invention and had just arrived from Geneva. He tore the letter to pieces. He had decided to attempt no more experiments. Then he wandered down to the Thames Embankment and sat beside the river for hours. The moon looked through a mane of golden-brown clouds like a lion’s eye. Countless stars glittered overhead like gold dust sprinkled across a purple dome. Now and then a barge swung out into the muddy current and drifted away with the tide, while the railway signals changed from green to bright red as trains shrieked across the bridge.

You will be glad to hear that the beginning of this enterprise, which has filled you with such dark expectations, has brought no disaster. I arrived here yesterday, and my first duty is to assure my dear sister that I am well and increasingly confident of success.

I am already far north of London. Walking through the streets of Petersburg, I feel a cold northern breeze against my cheeks that steadies my nerves and fills me with delight. Can you understand that feeling? This breeze has traveled from the regions I am approaching and offers me a first taste of their icy climate. Encouraged by this promising wind, my daydreams grow more intense and vivid. I cannot persuade myself to picture the pole as a place of frost and desolation. In my imagination it remains a realm of beauty and pleasure. There, Margaret, the sun is always visible, its broad disk grazing the horizon and casting an unending splendor. There—for, with your permission, sister, I will place some trust in earlier navigators—snow and frost are banished. Sailing across a calm sea, we may be carried to a land whose wonders and beauty surpass every inhabited region yet discovered. Its natural life and landscape may be unique, as the behavior of the heavenly bodies undoubtedly is in those unexplored solitudes. What might we not expect in a country of eternal light? There I may discover the marvelous force that draws the compass needle, and bring order to a thousand astronomical observations whose apparent irregularities need only this voyage to become consistent forever. I will satisfy my burning curiosity by seeing a part of the world no one has visited, and may walk on ground no human foot has ever marked. These prospects draw me onward. They are enough to overcome every fear of danger or death and make me begin this demanding voyage with the delight of a child setting off in a little boat with holiday companions to explore his native river. But even if all these guesses prove false, you cannot deny the immeasurable benefit I will bring humanity, down to its final generation, by finding a passage near the pole to countries that currently take many months to reach. Or I may uncover the secret of magnetism, which, if it can be discovered at all, can only be revealed through an undertaking like mine.

These thoughts have driven away the anxiety with which I began this letter. My heart glows with an enthusiasm that lifts me to heaven, for nothing calms the mind so well as a firm purpose: a point on which the soul can fix its intellectual gaze.
